title: Statistically Significant or Not?
intro: A study isn't “significant” as a whole. Each comparison in it is, or isn't.

learn.title: Same study, same participants
learn.text:
One survey can produce three significant findings and seven that aren't — from exactly the same people.

• Satisfaction 5.1 → 5.2 — a tiny effect, likely not significant
• Completion 55% → 85% — a large effect, likely significant

**Effect size** is why one clears the threshold and the other doesn't, with an identical sample.

try.q: Two findings come from the same survey and sample. Why is only one significant?
try.explain: Effect size is the deciding factor here.

learn.title: The four inputs
learn.text:
**Sample size** — how much information you have
**Effect size** — how big the observed difference is
**Variability** — how consistent responses are; noisy data needs more people
**Confidence level** — the threshold your organisation agreed for calling a result real

try.q: Responses are very inconsistent across participants. What does that mean for the test?
try.explain: Variability is one of the four inputs.

learn.title: What significance doesn't tell you
learn.text:
Significance does **not** mean a result is large or important. The American Statistical Association warns explicitly against reading it that way.

Report the observed difference, the uncertainty and the practical consequence together.

And **set the threshold before the data.** Calabro used 90% confidence as the agreed standard in contexts where that level of risk was acceptable — agreed in advance, not chosen once the numbers were in.

try.q: Why set the confidence level before collecting data?
options: Otherwise the threshold follows the result
It determines the sample size only
try.explain: Choosing afterwards is how a finding gets talked over the line.

test.explain: Each comparison is significant or it isn't.

test.q: What does a significant result NOT tell you?
options: That the difference is large or important
That the difference is unlikely to be chance
test.explain: The ASA warns against that reading.

test.q: What should be reported alongside significance?
options: The difference, the uncertainty and the consequence
The p-value and the sample size
The method and the tool used
test.explain: Together, so the reader can judge practical meaning.

options: The agreed threshold for calling a result real
The probability the finding is true
The width of the confidence interval
test.explain: An organisational agreement, not a property of the data.

test.q: Which input is about how much information you have?
test.explain: More people, more information — but it's one factor of four.
